detail.name: Ability
detail.summary: Ability — costs, cooldowns, cast windows and targeting. Everything a game calls a "skill", a "spell", an "attack" or a "tool use" is the same shape: check whether it can run, pay for it, wait a moment, then do something. Writing that shape once means a new ability is data plus one function, and it is impossible to forget the cooldown. Resources are not owned here. You register a resolver once and Ability stops caring whether stamina lives in a profile, a component or a table:
examples:
Ability.define("dash", {
cooldown = 4,
cost = { stamina = 24 },
targeting = "direction",
cast = 0,
run = function(ctx) ... end,
})
Ability.use("player:1", "dash", { direction = look })

Ability.resources(function(subject, kind) return pool(subject, kind) end,
function(subject, kind, amount) spend(subject, kind, amount) end)

detail.name: Actor
detail.summary: Actor — state machines, perception and population, for things that think. Roblox teaches a bad habit: one script per NPC, each with its own `while true do task.wait() end`. Two hundred enemies become two hundred scheduler entries and a server that dies at forty. Here every actor is a table, every brain is a data-declared state machine, and all of them tick in one sliced group. Two hundred actors cost one connection and a quarter of them think per frame. The engine runs the machine. What the states mean is entirely yours.
examples: local wolf = Actor.spawn(model, "wolf", { home = position, leash = 130 })

functions.summary: Has this actor been pulled too far from where it belongs? The single most important guard against an enemy following a player across the whole map.

functions.name: Instance_:moveTo
functions.summary: Where an actor is trying to get to. Two modes, and the difference is visible from across a room. `direct` points the Humanoid at the goal and lets it walk. On flat ground that is indistinguishable from anything better and costs nothing. Put a rock in the way and the actor presses into it forever, which is the single most recognisable "amateur Roblox game" behaviour there is. `navigate` hands the goal to `Nav`, which computes a real path over Roblox's navmesh, follows the waypoints, notices when it is wedged and repaths. It costs a path computation per repath, which is why it is not simply always on: a swarm of thirty melee enemies in an open arena gains nothing and pays for all of it. Set `Actor.config.navigation = true`, or per actor in the spawn spec, to turn it on. Anything with a world worth navigating wants it.

detail.name: Anim
detail.summary: Anim — layered procedural animation with markers. Why not AnimationTrack and rbxassetid ------------------------------------- Authored animation needs the Animation Editor and an upload, which means a human in a GUI for every timing change. That is fine for a studio and fatal for an agent: the one thing that most needs iteration becomes the one thing that cannot be iterated. Here a clip is *data*. It works on R6 and R15, it needs no asset, and — the part that actually matters — it carries its own MARKERS. The frame a sword becomes dangerous lives in the same table as the pose that swings it. Move the pose, the hit window moves with it. That is what makes combat timing tunable without touching combat logic. This does not replace authored animation. When you have a real animator, keep the clip names and the marker names and swap the pose source; every system that listened for "hit" still works. Track convention (degrees) -------------------------- swing   forward/back — the primary axis of a limb spread  outward, away from the body twist   rotation about the limb's own axis, or torso yaw Usage -----
examples:
local anim = Anim.new(character)
anim:setLocomotion(Anim.profiles.grounded)
anim:onMarker(function(clip, marker) ... end)

local playback = anim:play("attack_1", { speed = 1.2 })
Anim.bind(anim)   -- drives it on the right loop for this context

functions.name: Animator:setRootMotion
functions.summary: Movement that comes from the animation instead of from the controller. A dodge that plays a roll while the controller applies an impulse is two systems guessing at the same distance, and they disagree: the roll ends early, or the body slides past the end of it. Root motion makes the clip the authority — the animation says how far the body travels and the controller does nothing. A clip declares it as a curve of offsets in the character's own space: Applied as a delta each frame rather than an absolute position, so it composes with whatever else is moving the character and never teleports it back to where the clip thought it started.

While that is still present it rewrites the same joints every frame and no render priority is late enough to beat it -- that was measured, not assumed.

detail.name: Assets
detail.summary: Assets — one way to name and produce content. Without this every game invents its own loading: one system clones from ReplicatedStorage, another builds a rig from a table, a third has ids baked into an `if` chain. Then nothing can be listed, nothing can be preloaded, and a missing asset is a nil three frames later instead of a named error. Three things an asset id can resolve to, and Assets does not care which: a definition   a plain table (stats, config) a template     an Instance in the tree, cloned on demand a builder      a function that constructs it (procedural rigs, props) Namespaces ---------- An id is `Namespace.Name`, or `Namespace.Group.Name`. The namespace picks the producer, so registering a producer once teaches the engine how to make every asset of that kind: Missing assets never crash. They log once, and `spawn` returns a visible magenta placeholder — because a silent nil is how a level ends up with invisible holes nobody notices until a player falls through one.
examples:
Assets.spawn("Enemy.Orc", CFrame.new(0, 5, 0))
Assets.spawn("Prop.Barrel", cframe)
local sword = Assets.build("Weapon.Sword")

Assets.producer("Enemy", function(id, def) return Rig.build(def.rig) end)
Assets.register("Enemy.Orc", { rig = { scale = 1.2, shape = "biped" } })

detail.name: Bench
detail.summary: Bench — measured cost, instead of a number from an empty room. Every performance figure this engine had came from a Studio session with one player standing still. That is not evidence about a server with thirty people and four thousand entities; it is evidence about an empty room. What this can and cannot measure -------------------------------- Roblox refuses to conjure a Player: `Players:CreateLocalPlayer` and `Instance.new("Player")` both fail on capability, which is measured and recorded in the platform notes. So this does not simulate clients. It simulates *load*: N moving anchors, N entities, N receivers for a proximity broadcast — the server-side costs that actually scale. Replication bandwidth and client frame time still need real players, and this module says so rather than implying otherwise.
examples:
Bench.run("entity.query.2000", function() ... end, 200)
Bench.suite()          -- the standard set
Bench.report()

functions.summary: Synthetic anchors, for streaming and proximity work. They move on separate circles at different speeds, because the interesting case is not "thirty players in one place" — it is thirty players spread out, each pulling a different chunk set, which is when a streamer thrashes.

detail.name: Capability
detail.summary: Capability — ask Roblox what exists instead of assuming. This module exists because of a specific, expensive afternoon. `Sky.install` set `Terrain.Decoration = true`. That property does not exist in every Roblox version; on 0.735 it throws. Because `install` is a straight run of property writes, that one line aborted everything after it — the water never got its reflectance and a warning nobody saw never printed. A cosmetic nicety silently took out the rest of the function, and the only symptom was that the world looked slightly wrong. Then the same shape of bug happened three more times in a row with audio: invented marketplace ids, then `rbxasset://` names written from memory. Each one compiled, passed the doctor, passed the tests, built cleanly, and failed at runtime in front of a person. The pattern is always the same. Code written from memory about what the platform offers is a guess, and a guess that survives every static check. --- What this does ----------------------------------------------------- `set` writes the property if it exists and records the miss if it does not. Nothing throws, nothing aborts the caller, and `Capability.missing()` lists everything this build refused so it can be reported rather than discovered. --- Where the answers come from ---------------------------------------- Probes are cheap and cached: the first question about a property costs one pcall, every later one is a table lookup. `forge capability probe` runs the same checks from outside and writes them to JSON, so an agent can read what this Roblox build supports *before* writing code against it — which is the whole point.
examples:
Capability.has("Terrain.Decoration")   -- false on this build
Capability.set(Workspace.Terrain, "Decoration", true)  -- safe either way

The important part is not that it avoids the error — it is that the caller *continues*, so one missing cosmetic property can no longer take out the twenty lines after it. Returns whether the write landed, for the callers that care.

detail.name: Catalog
detail.summary: Catalog — Creator Store models this project has verified. Generated by `forge toolbox curate`. Do not hand-edit; regenerate it. Where these came from matters as much as what they are. They are not search results: each one was taken from a pack that Roblox developers actually use, found by reading the developer forum, and the pack's creator, licence and source thread travel with every piece. Most of them are Synty — a professional low-poly studio whose packs Roblox paid to release free, under an official Roblox account. Every entry was loaded inside Studio, measured and scanned. `parts`, `meshes` and `size` are readings off the real thing after insertion, not descriptions. Every entry has no scripts, because anything carrying one was refused rather than stripped: free-model scripts are the most common way a Roblox game gets backdoored, and deciding automatically which ones a model "needs" is exactly how that ships. An id absent from this file has not been checked, and `Assets` refuses it.
examples: local Catalog = Forge.Catalog

local trees = Catalog.byCategory("foliage")
local model = Catalog.load(trees[1])

detail.name: Collab
detail.summary: Collab — more than one person editing without ruining each other's work. The Editor has always assumed a single author. Two people in the same session both grab the same rock, both move it, and the second write wins silently — no conflict, no warning, and the first person's work is simply gone. That is the failure that makes teams stop using a tool. Three mechanisms, in the order they matter: leases    one editor owns a placement at a time, and the claim expires presence  everyone can see who is here and what they are holding journal   every change is attributed, so a mistake can be traced --- Why leases rather than locks ----------------------------------------- A lock is held until released, which means a lock is held forever the first time somebody's Studio crashes while holding one. A lease expires. Editors renew what they are actively using and everything else falls free on its own, so the recovery path for a crash is "wait twenty seconds" rather than "find an administrator". --- Authority ------------------------------------------------------------- Server only, and every function refuses to run on a client. A lease that a client could grant itself is not a lease, and the whole point is to be the one place that arbitrates between two people who both want the same thing.
examples:
if Collab.claim(player, placement) then
Editor.setCFrame(placement, target)
Collab.record(player, "move", placement)
end

functions.name: Collab.keyFor
functions.summary: A stable name for the thing being edited. Placements carry an id; instances are identified by their full path. Both are strings, which is what lets one table arbitrate over both without knowing which kind of editor is asking.

functions.name: Collab.claim
functions.summary: Take ownership, or find out who has it. Re-claiming something you already hold renews it rather than failing: an editor dragging a rock calls this every frame, and a claim that refused its own owner would make dragging impossible.

functions.name: Collab.startSweeper
functions.summary: Drop leases nobody renewed. Without this, every crashed or disconnected editor leaves its work locked until the server restarts, which in practice means people work around the system rather than with it.

functions.name: Collab.here
functions.summary: Who is editing, and what they are looking at. Cheap and worth far more than it costs: most collisions are avoided by knowing somebody else is already in that corner of the map, long before any lease has to refuse anything.

functions.summary: What changed, by whom. Not undo — the Editor has its own stack for that. This is the answer to "who moved the spawn point", which on a team is asked far more often and is otherwise unanswerable.

detail.name: Combat
detail.summary: Combat — mechanism for hurting things. Never policy about what hurting means. The distinction is the whole design. Combat knows how to find what is in front of a sword, how to run a damage number through a chain of modifiers, how to keep a status effect ticking and how to fly a projectile. It does not know what armour is, whether crits exist, or how your game scales damage by level — you install those as modifiers, and they compose. Then a hit is: Modifiers run in ascending order. Order is explicit because "armour before or after crit" changes balance and should never be an accident of table iteration.
examples:
Combat.addModifier("armor", 100, function(ctx)
local armor = ctx.target:GetAttribute("Armor") or 0
ctx.amount *= 100 / (100 + armor)
end)

Combat.addModifier("crit", 200, function(ctx)
if ctx.rng and ctx.rng:bool(ctx.critChance or 0) then
ctx.amount *= 1.85
ctx.crit = true
end
end)

local hits = Combat.arc(root.Position, look, { range = 9, angle = 110 })
for _, model in hits do
Combat.damage(model, { amount = 24, source = player, critChance = 0.1 })
end

detail.name: Core
detail.summary: !strict Core — primitives with no Roblox opinions in them. Everything here is testable without a DataModel, which is why it is separate.

detail.name: Data
detail.summary: Data — content tables with a declared shape. Balance lives in data, not in code. That is easy to say and hard to keep: six weeks in, half the numbers are inline in a system somewhere and the other half are in a table nobody validates, so a typo'd `dmg` silently becomes `nil` and a sword does zero damage in production. Data fixes the second half. You declare the shape once; every entry is checked at load with an error that names the file, the id and the field. `extends` gives variants without copy-paste:
examples: local Data = Forge.Data

Data.define("weapon", {
name    = { type = "string" },
damage  = { type = "number", min = 0 },
speed   = { type = "number", default = 1 },
rarity  = { type = "string", oneOf = { "common", "rare", "epic" } },
onHit   = { type = "table", optional = true },
})
Data.load("weapon", require(script.Weapons))
local sword = Data.get("weapon", "iron_sword")
iron_sword_plus = { extends = "iron_sword", damage = 22 }

functions.name: Data.setStrict
functions.summary: In strict mode a bad entry is an error. Turn it off only in a live session where you would rather limp than crash.

functions.name: Data.expect
functions.summary: Same as get, but a missing id is an error rather than nil. Use in systems where a nil would fail three call frames later with no useful message.

functions.name: Data.query
functions.signature: Data.query(kind: string, predicate: (entry: any, id: string) -> boolean)

functions.name: Data.snapshot
functions.summary: A snapshot a validator can diff between builds to see what balance changed.

functions.name: Data.describe
functions.summary: Debug.snapshot() collects `describe` from every module; without this one the entire content layer would be invisible to a validator.

detail.name: Debug
detail.summary: Debug — how a running game explains itself. This is the seam between the two halves. The Quality Engine's bridge can already measure geometry: raycasts, bounds, overlaps, part counts. What it cannot see is *meaning* — whether the economy is solvent, whether forty actors are stuck in one state, whether anyone has taken damage in the last minute. Those are facts only the game knows. Debug makes the game say them out loud, in JSON, through a replicated StringValue the plugin can read while the place is running. No loadstring, which does not exist in a play session anyway. Then from the validator, with a command that already exists: It also carries live tunables, so a number can be changed in a running session and the effect observed without a rebuild — the shortest iteration loop the platform allows.
examples:
dm.properties { path = "ReplicatedStorage.ForgeDebug.Snapshot",
properties = { "Value" } }

functions.name: Debug.probe
functions.summary: ================================= probes =================================== Register anything the game knows that a validator could not infer.

functions.name: Debug.count
functions.summary: =============================== counters =================================== Cheap event tallies: "damage dealt", "items dropped", "quests completed". A counter that stays at zero through a whole playtest is a system that never ran, which is the most common silent failure in a generated game.

functions.name: Debug.log
functions.signature: Debug.log(level: string, message: string, detail: any?)

functions.name: Debug.check
functions.signature: Debug.check(condition: boolean, description: string, detail: any?)
functions.summary: A soft assertion. It does not stop the game; it records a violated expectation so a playtest can end with a list of things that were not true. This is deliberately not `assert`. In a live session a hard error hides every problem after the first one.

functions.name: Debug.tunable
functions.summary: A number that can be changed while the game runs. The getter is a function so the value is read fresh every time. Capture it into a local once and you have silently opted out of tuning.
examples:
local cooldown = Debug.tunable("combat.attackCooldown", 0.55)
if now - last < cooldown() then return end

functions.name: Debug.snapshot
functions.summary: Everything the game can say about itself right now. Shape is stable on purpose: a validator diffs snapshots across builds, and a field that moves is a field that breaks the comparison.

functions.name: Debug.expose
functions.summary: Publishes the game's self-description where a validator can read it. This is a StringValue, not a BindableFunction, and the reason matters: **a BindableFunction does not cross the client/server boundary.** Its OnInvoke is bound in whichever Lua VM created it, so a server-side handler is simply absent from the client's VM and every invocation returns nil. The Studio plugin's `client.invoke_bindable` runs client-side, which made the first version of this seam look wired and return null forever. A replicated StringValue has no such problem. `dm.properties` reads it in *any* context -- edit, run, server or client -- using a command that already exists, with no new plugin surface: `Command` is the write side. Set it with `instance.update` (run context) to a JSON object and the answer appears in `Result`: The BindableFunction is still created for callers inside the same VM, where it is the more direct route.
examples:
dm.properties { path = "ReplicatedStorage.ForgeDebug.Snapshot",
properties = { "Value" } }

detail.name: Destruction
detail.summary: Destruction — things coming apart, on a budget. Every game wants breakable scenery and almost none ship it, because the naive version is a trap: a crate that shatters into forty unanchored parts is forty new physics bodies, replicated to every client, and a room full of crates is a server that stops. The interesting problem is not how to break something — it is how to break a hundred things and still hold a frame. So the whole module is built around a budget: * a global cap on live debris, oldest recycled first; * shards that sleep and anchor once they stop moving, so their physics * a fade and a lifetime, because debris that persists is debris that --- What this deliberately does not do ----------------------------------- Real fracture. Voronoi shattering of arbitrary geometry is expensive to compute and worse to replicate, and at Roblox's scale nobody can tell it from a handful of well-thrown boxes tinted to match. The shards here are sampled from the source object's own parts, so a stone crate throws stone and a wooden one throws wood without anybody authoring either.
examples: cost is one frame each rather than forever;
accumulates for the whole session.
Destruction.break_(crate, { from = hitPosition })

functions.name: Destruction.break_
functions.summary: Break something apart. The shards inherit colour and material from the object's own parts, so a stone wall throws stone and a wooden crate throws wood with nothing authored per object. `from` is where the blow came from: debris that flies away from the impact reads as caused, debris that flies in every direction reads as an explosion. Returns how many shards were actually made, which is not always what was asked for — the budget has the final say.

detail.name: Dialogue
detail.summary: Dialogue — conversation as a graph of data. Conditions gate choices, so a line that should not exist yet simply is not offered — rather than being offered and then refused, which reads as a bug to a player. Actions are names, not functions: the game registers what `"quests"` or `"shop"` means once, and every NPC reuses it.
examples:
local node = Dialogue.begin("player:1", "elder")
node = Dialogue.choose("player:1", 2)

functions.name: Dialogue.action
functions.summary: The game teaches Forge what an action name means, once.

functions.name: Dialogue.begin
functions.signature: Dialogue.begin(subject: string, treeId: string, context: any?)

functions.name: Dialogue.choose
functions.summary: `index` is the index the client was *shown*, taken from the offered list — not the raw index in the definition. A client that sends a raw index could otherwise pick a choice its own conditions hid, which is a trivial exploit in every dialogue system that forgets it.

detail.name: Ease
detail.summary: !strict Ease — curves by name, so a curve choice can live in a data table instead of in code. `Ease.get("outBack")(t)` is what makes a designer-tunable UI possible.

functions.name: Ease.lerp
functions.signature: Ease.lerp(a: any, b: any, t: number)
functions.summary: Lerp that works on the types gameplay actually interpolates.

functions.name: Ease.approach
functions.signature: Ease.approach(current: any, goal: any, speed: number, dt: number)
functions.summary: Frame-rate independent approach. `speed` is roughly "fraction closed per second". Use instead of `x += (goal - x) * 0.1`, which is frame-rate bound.

detail.name: Editor
detail.summary: Editor — the authoring surface over a Scene. Two callers, one API. A person clicking in the overlay and an agent calling `Editor.place("Prop.Barrel", cf)` go through exactly the same operations, which is the only way the UI and the automation can stay in agreement. The server is the only mutator. Editor operations arrive as one rate-limited event and are refused unless the sender is authorised — an editor reachable by any client is a griefing tool, and "we will remember to gate it later" is how that ships. Undo is real: every operation records its inverse before applying. A place undoes to a delete, a move undoes to the previous CFrame.
examples:
Editor.open(scene)
Editor.place("Prop.Barrel", CFrame.new(10, 3, 0))
Editor.select(placement)
Editor.nudge(Vector3.new(4, 0, 0))
Editor.rotate(45)
Editor.undo()
local json = Editor.save()

functions.name: Editor.toVector
functions.summary: Coerce a position that arrived from anywhere. The overlay sends a real Vector3 from a raycast. An agent driving the bridge sends JSON, so the same field arrives as `{30, 34, 24}` or `{x = 30, y = 34, z = 24}`. Without this, "the UI and automation go through the same operations" is a claim that only holds for callers already inside Luau — which was true of this file until a bridge test proved it was not.

functions.name: Editor.place
functions.signature: Editor.place(assetId: string, cframe: CFrame, options: any?)

functions.name: Editor.setLocked
functions.summary: Locked things cannot be selected by clicking, which is what makes editing a dense scene possible: terrain dressing stops fighting you for every click. Hidden things stay in the scene data and leave the world.

functions.name: Editor.paste
functions.summary: Paste keeps the relative arrangement of what was copied. Pasting each piece at the cursor collapses a copied camp into one point, which is the version of paste nobody wants twice.

functions.name: Editor.rotate
functions.signature: Editor.rotate(degrees: number, axis: string?, placement: any?)
functions.summary: Rotation about the selection's own centre, not about each piece's origin. Rotating each piece independently spins them in place and leaves the arrangement untouched, which is never what "rotate this camp" means.

functions.name: Editor.scale
functions.summary: Scale. `Model:ScaleTo` is the only uniform scale Roblox offers and not every model accepts it, so the factor is recorded in the placement as well: a scene reloaded from JSON reproduces the size even where the live call failed.

functions.name: Editor.groundPlacement
functions.summary: Drop a placement onto whatever is under it. The single most used editor action, and the one people otherwise do by eye and get wrong by half a stud.

functions.name: Editor.selectPlacement
functions.summary: Selection is a list, not a slot. Single selection is the special case of a list with one entry, and building it the other way round means multi-select arrives as a rewrite of every operation rather than as a loop. Every op below applies to the whole selection; `Editor.primary()` is the one the inspector shows.

functions.name: Editor.selectGroupOf
functions.summary: Everything in a placed prefab, from any one of its pieces. Selecting a tent and getting the camp is what makes group editing usable.

functions.name: Editor.selectionCentre
functions.summary: The centre of the selection, which is what a gizmo anchors to.

functions.name: Editor.search
functions.summary: Everything matching a substring of its asset id or name. The only practical way to find one placement among four hundred.

functions.name: Editor.serve
functions.summary: One event, one switch. A separate remote per operation is a wider surface to authorise and an easier one to forget.

detail.name: Entity
detail.summary: Entity — composition instead of inheritance. The problem this solves ----------------------- A framework grows systems that know what a Player is and what an NPC is. Then you want a destructible barrel that has health but no brain, a turret that fights but never moves, a chest that can be interacted with but is not a creature — and every system needs a new special case. That is the point where a framework stops scaling and a game becomes a pile of `if`. Here nothing is a Player or an NPC. Things are entities, and an entity is whatever components it carries. `Combat` operates on anything with Health. `Movement` operates on anything with a Transform and a Motor. A barrel is an entity with Health and no Brain, and no system needed changing. This is not a full archetype ECS, and deliberately so: in Luau the cache wins of archetype storage do not materialise, while the complexity does. Component stores keyed by entity id give the decoupling, which is the part that actually matters. Instances --------- Roblox is instance-based, so an entity may own one. The link is two-way and self-cleaning: destroy the instance and the entity goes with it.
examples:
Entity.define("Health", { max = 100, current = 100, dead = false })
Entity.define("Brain",  { state = "idle", target = nil })

local orc = Entity.create({ name = "Orc", instance = model })
Entity.add(orc, "Health", { max = 240, current = 240 })
Entity.add(orc, "Brain")

for id, health in Entity.query("Health") do
if health.current <= 0 then Entity.destroy(id) end
end

functions.name: Entity.define
functions.signature: Entity.define(component: string, defaults: any?, options: any?)
functions.summary: Declaring a component is declaring its default shape. Defaults are deep copied per entity, so two orcs never share one Health table — the single most common bug in a hand-rolled component system.

functions.name: Entity.add
functions.signature: Entity.add(id: Id, component: string, data: any?)

functions.name: Entity.ensure
functions.signature: Entity.ensure(id: Id, component: string, data: any?)
functions.summary: Get, creating with defaults if absent. For systems that want to assume.

functions.name: Entity.serializeAll
functions.summary: Every persistable entity in one call, for a world save.

functions.name: Entity.query
functions.summary: Iterate every entity carrying all the named components: The rarest component drives the loop, so a query over 3 turrets and 4000 props costs three checks, not four thousand.
examples: for id, health, brain in Entity.query("Health", "Brain") do ... end

functions.name: Entity.queryOrdered
functions.summary: The same, in ascending id order. Use it when the order must be reproducible — a deterministic replay, a snapshot a validator diffs between runs. It pays a sort over the driving set, so do not reach for it in a per-frame system.

functions.name: Entity.system
functions.signature: Entity.system(name: string, components: { string }, fn: (dt: number, ...any) -> (), options: SystemOptions?)

detail.name: Events
detail.summary: Events — the spine everything else listens to. Why a second event system, when Signal exists --------------------------------------------- Signal connects one producer to its consumers. Events is a *namespace*: the combat system emits `enemy.killed` without knowing that quests, achievements, analytics, the tutorial and a leaderboard are all listening. That is the difference between systems that compose and systems that have to import each other. It is also what makes objective tracking generic. `Quest` does not know what a kill is; it knows how to count events matching a filter. Adding a new objective type becomes adding a line of data, not a branch in a tracker. Every emission is recorded in a ring buffer, so a playtest can be asked what actually happened rather than what was supposed to.
examples: Events.emit("enemy.killed", { by = player, kind = "orc", at = position })

Events.on("enemy.killed", function(payload) ... end)
Events.onAny(function(name, payload) ... end)

functions.name: Events.on
functions.signature: Events.on(name: string, fn: (payload: any, name: string) -> (), filter: ((payload: any) -> boolean)?)
functions.summary: `filter` narrows without a branch in your handler, which is what lets a quest say "orcs only" as data:
examples: Events.on("enemy.killed", tally, function(p) return p.kind == "orc" end)

functions.name: Events.once
functions.signature: Events.once(name: string, fn: (payload: any, name: string) -> (), filter: ((payload: any) -> boolean)?)

functions.name: Events.audit
functions.summary: Every event name that has ever fired, plus every name anyone listens for. The difference between the two sets is almost always a bug: a listener waiting on an event nobody emits, or an event nobody hears.

detail.name: Examples
detail.summary: Examples — one runnable demonstration per module. A documented example rots. It is written once, the API moves, and nobody notices until an agent copies it and gets an error. This project has been bitten by that exact shape all day: a comment describing a call that was no longer true is worse than no comment, because it is believed. So these are not snippets in a docstring. Each one is a function that actually runs inside the live game, does the thing, asserts something small about the result, and cleans up after itself. `forge example --all` runs every one of them; if the API moves, the example fails, and it fails in CI rather than in an agent's hands. --- What an example is for ---------------------------------------------- Not test coverage — `Testing` does that, and these deliberately assert almost nothing. An example answers "what does using this module look like", which is the question an agent has when it has never seen the engine and is deciding whether a module is the right tool. That is why each one is short, uses the shortest path through its module, and reads top to bottom.
examples:
forge example Combat      run one
forge example --all       run all of them

functions.name: Examples.run
functions.summary: Run one example and report what happened. Failures are returned rather than thrown: running twenty examples and stopping at the first broken one hides the other nineteen, and the whole point is to find out which parts of the surface have drifted.

detail.name: Feel
detail.summary: Feel — impact, weight and reaction. This is the module that decides whether a game reads as professional. Two games with identical mechanics, one with hitstop and screen shake and damage numbers that arc, one without — players will describe the first as "polished" and the second as "unfinished", and neither will be able to say why. It is also the layer agents skip, because nothing breaks without it. So it ships here, in the engine, as one call per effect. Camera shake here is trauma-based and noise-driven, not random jitter. Trauma decays, and offset scales with trauma squared, so small hits barely register and big ones hit hard — the difference between shake that feels like impact and shake that feels like a loose cable.
examples:
Feel.mount()                              -- once, on the client
Feel.shake(0.6)                           -- trauma, 0..1
Feel.hitstop(0.08)                        -- the pause that sells a hit
Feel.number(pos, "142", { crit = true })
Feel.impact(pos, { color = c, kind = "burst" })
Feel.flash(model, Color3.new(1,1,1), 0.1)
Feel.knockback(model, direction, 40)

functions.name: Feel.shake
functions.summary: Adds trauma rather than setting it, so three hits in a frame compound.

functions.name: Feel.hitstop
functions.summary: A short pause on impact. Registered animators freeze; everything else keeps running, which is what makes it read as weight rather than as lag.

functions.name: Feel.punch
functions.summary: FOV punch: small, fast, and the cheapest way to sell a heavy hit.

functions.name: Feel.mount
functions.summary: Installs the per-frame driver. Call once from a client script. It writes to `camera.CFrame` after the default camera script has run, so it composes with whatever camera mode the game uses instead of fighting it.

functions.name: Feel.number
functions.signature: Feel.number(position: Vector3, text: string, options: any?)
functions.summary: A number that rises, drifts sideways and fades. The sideways drift is what stops a burst of hits from stacking into an unreadable column — it is a two-line detail that decides whether the player can read their own DPS.

functions.name: Feel.impact
functions.summary: kind: "burst"  omnidirectional spark — generic hit "spray"  directional, needs options.direction — slashes, bullet impacts "ring"   expanding disc — slams, shockwaves, spawns "puff"   slow soft cloud — dust, landings, footfalls

functions.name: Feel.flash
functions.signature: Feel.flash(model: Model, color: Color3?, duration: number?)
functions.summary: ============================= character feedback =========================== White flash on hit. Restores the original colours, so it is safe to stack.

functions.name: Feel.knockback
functions.signature: Feel.knockback(model: Model, direction: Vector3, force: number, upward: number?)
functions.summary: Impulse-based knockback that respects mass, so a golem shrugs off what staggers a rat without any per-enemy special case.

functions.name: Feel.screenTint
functions.signature: Feel.screenTint(color: Color3, intensity: number, duration: number?)
functions.summary: A brief full-screen tint. Damage taken, healing, level up.

functions.name: Feel.breathing
functions.signature: Feel.breathing(character: Model, on: boolean, options: any?)
functions.summary: Keep breathing until stopped. Interval jitters slightly: a puff on an exact metronome reads as a machine. Real panting slows as it recovers, which the caller can drive by changing `interval` on the fly.

functions.name: Feel.hit
functions.summary: One call for the common case: something got hit here, sell it. Keeps the four things that always go together from drifting apart.

detail.name: Gizmo
detail.summary: Editor.Gizmo — the 3D manipulators. This is the difference between a tool and an admin panel. Nudging with arrow keys is fine for a final half-stud; placing a camp means grabbing a handle and dragging it, and no amount of keyboard shortcuts substitutes for that. Built on Roblox's own `Handles` and `ArcHandles`, which render real depth-sorted 3D manipulators and give back drag distances in world units — so this file is mostly about turning those into editor operations. Three modes, one keystroke apart: move    W    axis arrows rotate  E    orbit rings scale   R    resize handles Multi-select is why the handles are adorned to a proxy part at the selection centre rather than to a placement's own model: dragging then moves the whole set together, and rotation happens about the group's middle.

functions.name: Gizmo.setTarget
functions.summary: Point the gizmo at a world position, or hide it. Called whenever the selection changes. `nil` means nothing is selected, and a gizmo floating over nothing is worse than no gizmo.

functions.name: Gizmo.mount
functions.summary: `parent` must be the PlayerGui itself, not a Frame inside a ScreenGui. `Handles` and `ArcHandles` are GuiBase3d adornments. Parented into a 2D GUI hierarchy they are accepted, never render, and never fire a drag — the feature looks wired from the code and does not exist in the world. Only querying the running session for the instances found it.

detail.name: IK
detail.summary: IK — putting a hand or a foot where the world is, not where the clip said. Forward kinematics, which is everything this engine has done so far, works from the shoulder outwards: you choose angles and the hand ends up wherever that puts it. It is exact, cheap and completely blind to the world. A walk clip authored on flat ground puts a foot six inches into a slope, and a two-handed grip authored for one weapon misses the next one. Inverse kinematics runs the other way: you name the point the hand or foot must reach and it solves for the angles. Two bones and a hinge is the whole problem, and it has a closed-form answer — no iteration, no solver, no per-frame cost worth measuring. --- Where this sits ------------------------------------------------------ IK runs *after* the animator has posed the skeleton, as a correction. That order matters: the clip still decides what the body is doing, and this only adjusts the last two bones of a limb so the end lands correctly. Running it first, or instead, gives you a character that reaches things beautifully and has no performance. R15 only, and honestly so. An R6 rig has no elbow or knee, so there is no second bone to solve for and nothing here can help it.
examples:
IK.footPlant(character, { maxDrop = 3 })     -- feet follow the ground
IK.reach(character, "right", targetPosition) -- hand goes to a point

functions.name: IK.solveTwoBone
functions.signature: IK.solveTwoBone(upper: number, lower: number, distance: number)
functions.summary: Solve a two-bone chain. Given the length of the upper and lower bone and the straight-line distance to the target, the law of cosines gives both joint angles directly. Returns the shoulder-side and elbow-side angles in radians. The clamp is the important part. If the target is further than both bones can reach, the honest answer is "point straight at it and fall short" — the alternative is a NaN from `math.acos` of something greater than one, which propagates into a CFrame and makes the whole limb vanish.

functions.name: IK.reach
functions.signature: IK.reach(character: Model, side: string, target: Vector3, options: any?)
functions.summary: Put a hand on a point in the world. Used for the thing that has been visibly wrong in this project all day: a second hand that should be on the bow and is instead near it. With a solved elbow the hand goes *to* the grip rather than approximately toward it, and the same call works for a ladder rung, a door handle or a ledge. Returns whether the point was reachable. A caller that ignores that will happily animate a character straining at something two studs too far away.

functions.name: IK.holdWith
functions.signature: IK.holdWith(character: Model, side: string, attachment: BasePart, offset: Vector3?)
functions.summary: Hold a hand on a gripped object, every frame. The off hand of a two-handed weapon is the classic case: the weapon is welded to one hand and the other has to follow it wherever the animation takes it. Solved rather than authored, it stays correct for every clip and every weapon, including ones written later.

functions.name: IK.lift
functions.summary: How much each planted foot is currently lifting. Exists to be measured. Foot IK has broken this project's character twice — once by overwriting the animation and once by folding the legs — and both times the symptom was visual and the cause was a number. A correction that reads above a few tenths of a stud on flat ground is wrong, and now that is checkable without looking at anything.

detail.name: Input
detail.summary: Input — actions, not keys. Roughly half of Roblox plays on a phone. A game that reads `UserInputService.InputBegan` and compares against `Enum.KeyCode.Q` has already decided it does not ship there, and usually nobody notices until the first mobile session shows a player who cannot dodge. So nothing in a game refers to a key. It refers to an action, and the action knows what it is on each device: Touch buttons are generated from the definitions. Declaring an action with a `touch` table is the entire mobile port for that action — there is no second implementation to keep in sync, which is the reason mobile support usually rots. Rebinding is free because the indirection already exists, and bindings persist per player.
examples:
local move = Input.axis("move")     -- WASD, thumbstick or joystick
if Input.isDown("block") then ... end

functions.name: Input.bind
functions.signature: Input.bind(name: string, handler: (phase: string, action: string) -> ())
functions.summary: phase is "begin" | "end". Returning true from a handler marks the input consumed, which is how a menu takes priority over gameplay without either knowing about the other.

functions.name: Input.axis
functions.summary: One movement vector regardless of device. Keyboard and gamepad come from the Humanoid's own MoveDirection so the engine never fights Roblox's control scripts; touch adds the virtual joystick on top.

functions.name: Input.rebind
functions.signature: Input.rebind(name: string, key: any, forDevice: string?)

functions.name: Input.label
functions.summary: Readable label for a binding, for a settings screen or a key prompt.

functions.name: Input.refresh
functions.summary: Rebuilds every binding. Cheap, and called whenever an action is added or a key is rebound, so there is no path where the live bindings disagree with the table.

functions.name: Input.unmount
functions.summary: Tear everything down. Needed by tests and by any flow that rebuilds the client shell without a rejoin; without it a second `mount` stacks a second joystick on the first.

detail.name: Interaction
detail.summary: Interaction — things a player can do to the world, in one registry. This wraps ProximityPrompt, and the wrapping earns its place entirely because of two measured Roblox behaviours that silently break interaction and are invisible in the code that causes them: * `ProximityPromptExclusivity` defaults to `OnePerButton`, so the nearest * `InputHoldBegin()` from the server is accepted and `Triggered` never A prompt on a fast unanchored part also never fires; the registry warns rather than leaving you to find out.
examples:
Interaction.register(chestModel, {
id = "chest",
label = "Open",
holdDuration = 0.4,
range = 12,
onTrigger = function(player, instance) ... end,
})

prompt sharing a key **suppresses every other one**. A prompt can be
visible, in range, enabled and impossible to trigger. Forge sets
`AlwaysShow` and hands out distinct keys.

fires. Activation is client-side, so a headless test that "triggers" a
prompt server-side proves nothing. `Interaction.trigger` exists for
tests and calls the handler directly, honestly, without pretending a
prompt fired.

functions.name: Interaction.trigger

detail.name: LiveOps
detail.summary: LiveOps — changing a running game without shipping a new one. A game that can only be changed by publishing is a game whose every balance tweak costs a release and whose every mistake costs a rollback. Everything here exists so a number can be moved, a feature can be switched off, or an experiment can be started, while people are playing. Four things, because they are one mechanism wearing four hats: config   a value the server reads instead of a constant flags    a config value that is a boolean, with a kill switch bucket   a config value chosen per player, which is an experiment text     a config value chosen per locale, which is localisation --- Where the values come from ----------------------------------------- A real DataStore, read on an interval, with the last good values kept in memory. That ordering matters more than it looks: a DataStore outage must never take the game down, so a failed refresh leaves the previous values in place and says so. A config system that fails closed turns a Roblox incident into your incident. --- Bucketing -------------------------------------------------------------- Assignment is a hash of the player's id and the experiment name, not a random roll. A player therefore lands in the same arm on every server, on every session, forever — which is the difference between an experiment and noise. It also means no state has to be stored to remember the decision.
examples:
LiveOps.define("enemy.maxAlive", 14)
LiveOps.flag("newLootTable", false)
LiveOps.experiment("firstSessionLength", { "control", "longer" })

local cap = LiveOps.get("enemy.maxAlive")
if LiveOps.enabled("newLootTable") then ... end
local arm = LiveOps.bucket(player, "firstSessionLength")

functions.name: LiveOps.define
functions.summary: Declare a value and its default. The default is the contract: it is what the game runs on with no network, on the first frame, and whenever the store disagrees about types. Declaring up front also means `describe()` can list every knob a game has, which is what makes this auditable rather than a bag of magic strings.

functions.name: LiveOps.get
functions.summary: Read a value. Remote wins over default, but only when it is the same type. A config push that turns a number into a string would otherwise propagate a type error into gameplay code minutes after the deploy that caused it, which is the worst possible place to find it.

functions.name: LiveOps.kill
functions.summary: Turn something off right now. Local only, and deliberately: a kill switch that has to round-trip to a DataStore before it takes effect is not a kill switch. Pushing the same value remotely is how it becomes permanent.

functions.name: LiveOps.experiment
functions.signature: LiveOps.experiment(name: string, arms: { string }, options: any?)

functions.name: LiveOps.strings
functions.summary: Translated text, by locale. Not a wrapper over Roblox's translation tables on purpose: those are authored in Studio and shipped with the place, which puts a typo fix behind a release. These live in the same config the rest of this module reads, so a wrong string is fixed in the time it takes to write it. `LiveOps.text` always returns something. A missing key returns the key itself, which renders as visible nonsense in the UI — far better than an empty label, because it is impossible to miss in testing.

functions.name: LiveOps.refresh
functions.summary: Pull the live values. Server only. A client that read config directly would be a client that can be told a different config, and every value here is a value somebody would like to choose for themselves.

detail.name: Material
detail.summary: Material — physically based surfaces. Everything this engine has rendered so far has been `Part.Material` and a colour: SmoothPlastic, Wood, Slate. Those are Roblox's *legacy* materials, and they carry no normal map, no roughness and no metalness. A rock made of them is a coloured box with a noise texture, and no amount of lighting work fixes it, because there is nothing in the surface for light to catch. Two mechanisms replace that, and they are for different things: `SurfaceAppearance` overrides one MeshPart's textures. It is how a specific model gets its own colour, normal, metalness and roughness maps. `MaterialVariant` replaces a whole legacy material everywhere at once. Register a variant named for `Enum.Material.Slate` and every Slate surface in the game — including terrain — picks it up. That is the lever worth pulling first, because it upgrades the entire world in one call without touching a single part. --- On ids --------------------------------------------------------------- Every texture id here goes through `Assets`, which refuses anything that has not been loaded successfully once. That is deliberate: a wrong texture id does not error, it renders as a flat grey surface, which is exactly the sort of silent failure that survives every static check and is discovered by a person squinting at a screenshot.
examples:
Material.define("mossy_rock", {
base = Enum.Material.Slate,
color = "rbxassetid://...",
normal = "rbxassetid://...",
roughness = "rbxassetid://...",
studsPerTile = 8,
})
Material.applyTerrain(Enum.Material.Slate, "mossy_rock")

functions.name: Material.define
functions.summary: Register a material variant. `base` is the legacy material it stands in for. That is not cosmetic: physics reads the base material for friction and density, and terrain can only carry a variant that names the terrain material it replaces.

functions.name: Material.defineMany
functions.summary: Define several, and report how many this build could actually take. Returns the count rather than nothing, so a caller can tell the difference between "PBR is on" and "PBR silently did nothing here" — which from a screenshot look identical.

functions.name: Material.applyTerrain
functions.summary: Make a legacy material render as a variant, everywhere. One call and every Slate surface in the world changes, terrain included. This is the highest-leverage thing in the module and the reason variants beat per-part appearances for world-scale work.

functions.name: Material.surface
functions.summary: Give one MeshPart its own textures. `SurfaceAppearance` is a child of the part, not a property, and a part may only have one — so an existing appearance is replaced rather than duplicated, which Roblox would otherwise refuse at runtime.

functions.name: Material.paint
functions.summary: Apply a defined material to a part and everything under it. Sets the base material as well as the variant name, because a part whose `MaterialVariant` names something its `Material` does not match renders as the plain base — a silent mismatch that looks like the texture failed to load.

functions.name: Material.renderFidelity
functions.summary: Render distance per model. Roblox has no author-facing LOD, but `MeshPart.RenderFidelity` is the part of it that matters most: `Precise` on every rock in a forest is how a scene with a good frame budget spends all of it on geometry nobody can see. `Automatic` lets Roblox drop fidelity with distance. It is almost always the right answer for scatter, and almost always the wrong one for anything the player stands next to.

functions.name: Material.shadowBudget
functions.summary: Stop small props from casting shadows. A shadow costs roughly what the geometry costs. On a pebble it buys nothing, and a field of scattered pebbles each casting one is a measurable share of a frame for detail no player will ever notice missing.

detail.name: Monetization
detail.summary: Monetization — passes, products and receipts that cannot double-grant. `ProcessReceipt` is the most dangerous callback in Roblox. Roblox retries it until it returns `PurchaseGranted`, which means: * return the wrong value and the player is charged and gets nothing; * grant without recording and a retry grants twice; * error inside the handler and Roblox keeps calling it, forever. So the grant and the record are one operation, keyed on the receipt's own `PurchaseId`, in a DataStore. That is the entire correctness story and it is not optional.
examples:
Monetization.prompt(player, "small_coins")
if Monetization.owns(player, "vip") then ... end

functions.name: Monetization.owns
functions.summary: Cached, because `UserOwnsGamePassAsync` is a web call and gameplay asks "does this player have VIP" in places that run every frame. The cache expires so a mid-session purchase is picked up without a rejoin.

functions.name: Monetization.processReceipt
functions.summary: The receipt handler, callable directly. Roblox owns the real one, which makes it unreachable from a test — and this is the one function in the engine whose bug costs money. Exposing it lets a live suite deliver the same receipt twice and assert that the grant happened once, which is the failure Roblox's retry behaviour causes routinely.

detail.name: Nav
detail.summary: Nav — getting from here to there without walking into things. Until now every actor in this engine moved by pointing itself at its target and calling `Humanoid:MoveTo`. On a flat arena that is invisible. On any world with a rock in it, the enemy walks into the rock and stays there, pressing forward forever, which is the single most recognisable "this is an amateur Roblox game" behaviour there is. This wraps Roblox's own `PathfindingService` — a real navmesh computed from the real world, not a grid this engine invented — and adds the parts that service leaves to you: * repathing when the target moves, throttled so a chasing enemy does not * waypoint following with a stuck detector, because a computed path is * a straight-line fallback, so a failed path degrades to the old --- On costs ------------------------------------------------------------ `AgentParameters` are the difference between an enemy that squeezes through a doorway and one that refuses to. They are exposed per agent rather than fixed, because a hulking brute genuinely does need a wider path than a stalker, and pretending otherwise is how you get a boss stuck on a fence.
examples: recompute a path sixty times a second;
not a guarantee that a Humanoid will actually traverse it;
behaviour instead of an actor standing still.

functions.name: Nav.computePath
functions.signature: Nav.computePath(from: Vector3, to: Vector3, parameters: any?)
functions.summary: Compute a path, or say why not. Returns the waypoint list and a status string. The status matters: a caller that treats "NoPath" the same as "Success with zero waypoints" will happily report that an actor has arrived when it never set off.

functions.name: Nav.reachable
functions.signature: Nav.reachable(from: Vector3, to: Vector3, parameters: any?)
functions.summary: Is there a walkable route at all? Cheap enough to ask before committing to a fight: an enemy that cannot reach the player should give up and go home rather than press against a wall until the session ends.

functions.name: Nav.follow
functions.summary: Put an actor on a path and keep it there. `target` may be a Vector3, a Model, or a function returning either — the function form is what makes chasing work, because the goal is re-read every step rather than captured once.

functions.name: Nav.start
functions.summary: One connection for every agent. The alternative — a coroutine per enemy — is the pattern this engine exists to avoid: two hundred actors become two hundred schedulable threads and the frame time stops being anybody's fault in particular.

functions.name: Nav.modifier
functions.signature: Nav.modifier(part: BasePart, label: string, passthrough: boolean?)
functions.summary: Mark something as a cost or a blocker for pathfinding. Roblox reads `PathfindingModifier` off parts, which is the only way to say "this is water, prefer to go around" or "this door is passable". Wrapped here so a game never has to name the class.

detail.name: Net
detail.summary: Net — a typed, validated, rate-limited bus between client and server. Roblox gives you RemoteEvent, which is a hole in your server. Every exploit that matters in a Roblox game goes through one: the client sends `{ price = 0 }` and the server believes it. The defence is not vigilance, it is making the unsafe path harder to write than the safe one. So: an event that is not declared does not exist, every client->server packet is shape-checked before your handler sees it, and every one is rate limited whether you remembered to think about it or not. Server: Client: Nothing here decides what your events mean. It only decides that they are declared, shaped and throttled.
examples:
Net.on("Attack", function(player, payload) ... end)
Net.fire(player, "StateSync", state)
Net.fireNear(position, 120, "Effect", fx)

Net.send("Attack", { dir = look })
Net.on("StateSync", function(state) ... end)
local stock = Net.request("GetShop", { shop = "smith" })

functions.signature: Net.fire(player: Player, name: string, payload: any?)

functions.name: Net.fireExcept
functions.signature: Net.fireExcept(excluded: Player, name: string, payload: any?)

functions.signature: Net.fireNear(position: Vector3, radius: number, name: string, payload: any?)
functions.summary: Only players within `radius` of `position` receive it. In an open world this is the difference between 20 KB/s and 400 KB/s per client, and it is the single highest-leverage networking decision in the whole engine.

functions.summary: ============================== listening =================================== One `on` for both sides. On the server the handler receives (player, payload) and only runs if the packet passed the gate; on the client it receives (payload).

functions.name: Net.describe

detail.name: Netcode
detail.summary: Netcode — prediction, reconciliation, lag compensation and interpolation. `Net` is the transport: typed, validated, rate limited. It says nothing about *time*, and time is the whole problem in an action game. Without this layer the loop is: which means every action costs a round trip. At 50ms nobody notices. At 150ms the swing lags the click. At 200ms it reads as rubber. With it: Four pieces, and each solves a different symptom: prediction      your own actions feel instant reconciliation  a rejected action is undone, not left desynced rewind          a hit that looked good on your screen counts interpolation   other people and enemies move smoothly, not in steps What this is not ---------------- It is not rollback netcode for a fighting game and does not pretend to be. Roblox owns the physics step and does not expose a deterministic rewind of the whole simulation. What it does is make *gameplay actions* feel local and *hit detection* fair, which is the part players feel.
examples: input -> server -> authoritative state -> client sees it

input -> predicted locally -> server authorises -> reconcile or roll back
-> remote entities interpolated behind time

functions.name: Netcode.latency
functions.summary: One-way latency estimate. Half the round trip, which is the standard approximation and wrong only when the route is asymmetric.

functions.name: Netcode.simulate
functions.summary: Test controls. Deliberately public: the whole point is being able to set 200ms from outside and watch what happens, without a build.

functions.name: Netcode.broadcastSimulation
functions.signature: Netcode.broadcastSimulation(latencyMs: number?, loss: number?, reset: boolean?)
functions.summary: Broadcast a simulation setting to every client. Server-side entry point for a latency sweep driven from outside the game.

functions.name: Netcode.positionAt
functions.summary: Where a model was at `when`, interpolated between the two nearest samples.

functions.name: Netcode.rewind
functions.summary: Run `fn` with every tracked model moved to where it was on `player`'s screen, then put everything back. The restore happens in a `pcall`-protected path: a handler that errors must not leave the world rewound, because the next frame would then simulate physics from a stale position.

functions.name: Netcode.wire
functions.summary: Create the netcode channel and start listening. Called at module load, not from `Netcode.define`. That ordering was the whole bug behind the latency sweep never reaching a client: * remotes are only instantiated on the server; * the server only reached `Netcode.define` inside `Fight.start()`, which * the client, which starts immediately, called `Net.on("NetcodeSim")` Under Studio's fast terrain it resolved and the sweep looked merely flaky; on a slower machine the wait expired and the client never heard a simulation instruction again for the whole session. Either way the existence of the engine's own channel was hostage to how long a game's world took to build. Wiring at load makes the remotes exist as soon as anything requires `Forge.Netcode`, which on the server is during the first line of the bootstrap. Still idempotent, because `define` also calls it.
examples: runs after terrain generation and takes seconds;

and sat in a bounded `WaitForChild` for a remote that did not exist

detail.name: Presets
detail.summary: Anim.Presets — a starter set of clips. Read this carefully, because it is the one file in Forge that comes closest to breaking the rule: these are EXAMPLES, not the engine. They exist so a new project has something moving in the first minute, and so there is a worked reference for how tracks and markers fit together. Copy them into your game and edit them. Do not build a game on top of the defaults and then wonder why it feels like every other game built on the defaults — that is exactly the failure mode Forge exists to avoid. Marker vocabulary used here (yours can differ, but be consistent): hit          the frame damage should be dealt trail_on/off weapon trail window telegraph    the moment the player must be able to read the attack iframes_on/off invulnerability window release      a projectile or effect leaves the caster fall         the body should go ragdoll / settle draw_full    a charged weapon has reached full power mag_out/in   the reload's two halves eject        a casing leaves the weapon grab         the object should change hands lifted       it is clear of the ground
examples:
local Anim = Forge.Anim
Anim.registerAll(require(Anim.Presets))   -- then override what you want

detail.summary: Progression — levels, experience, points and unlocks, for any subject. "Subject" and not "player" on purpose: the same machinery levels a weapon, a settlement, a pet or a skill tree. A game that hard-codes progression to players has to write it again the first time a sword gains levels.
examples:
local track = Progression.track("hero", "player:" .. userId)
Progression.award(track, 320)

Progression.totals(track).health   -- accumulated per-level grants
Progression.unlocked(track, "ability.dash")

detail.name: Quest
detail.summary: Quest — objectives as event filters. The design decision that makes this generic: an objective does not have a *kind*. It has an event name and a match. "Kill five orcs", "collect eight pelts", "reach the summit" and "survive three nights" are the same mechanism with different data, so adding a new objective type is adding a line of content, not a branch in a tracker. `useAmount` counts the payload's `amount` rather than one per event, which is the difference between "picked up 4 pelts at once" counting as 4 or as 1.
examples: Quest.accept("player:1", "q_wolves")

functions.name: Quest.available
functions.summary: Can this subject take this quest right now? Checks prerequisites and the repeat rule, so callers never have to re-derive the chain logic.

functions.name: Quest.objectiveDone
functions.signature: Quest.objectiveDone(questId: string, objectiveId: string, progress: number)

functions.summary: One wildcard listener drives every quest for every subject. The alternative — one listener per active objective — means a server with fifty players running six quests each carries three hundred subscriptions that must be torn down exactly right on abandon, completion and disconnect. This costs one dispatch per event and cannot leak.

functions.name: Quest.complete
functions.summary: Hand in a fulfilled quest. Rewards are returned rather than granted: Quest does not know what gold is, or where a player's inventory lives. The caller applies them, which keeps this module free of every other system.

functions.name: Quest.journal
functions.summary: Everything a quest log needs, already shaped for display.

detail.name: Rig
detail.summary: Rig — characters authored in code. A creature's silhouette becomes a table of numbers. That matters for two reasons: an agent can create a new enemy without a modelling tool, and the difference between a rat and a golem becomes something you can tune rather than something you have to re-model. R6 by default: six joints, and `shape` changes the posture rather than the bone count -- a quadruped is an R6 rig with a pitched torso, which reads correctly and costs nothing. `rigType = "R15"` builds the fifteen-part skeleton instead, with elbows, knees, wrists and ankles. That exists because shoulders alone can only aim an arm, never fold one, and an archer's draw hand belongs at the cheek.
examples:
local model = Rig.build({
name = "Grass Wolf",
scale = 0.85,
shape = "quadruped",
body = Color3.fromRGB(112, 106, 96),
accent = Color3.fromRGB(64, 60, 54),
eyes = Color3.fromRGB(240, 200, 80),
weapon = nil,
})

functions.name: Rig.attachWeapon
functions.signature: Rig.attachWeapon(model: Model, kind: string, color: Color3, scale: number)
functions.summary: Put a weapon in a rig's hand. Kept as the short form used by `Rig.build`'s `weapon` field; it is `buildWeapon` plus `grip` and nothing else. It used to be a second, subtly different way to assemble a weapon, which is how enemies ended up holding blades at a believable angle and players holding them at none.

functions.name: Rig.grip
functions.signature: Rig.grip(character: Model, thing: Instance, options: any?)

functions.name: Rig.buildWeapon
functions.summary: Weapons built in code, as models with a `Grip` primary part. They exist because a shooting system whose weapons are invisible is a shooting system nobody believes. These are simple assemblies of boxes, and they are meant to be replaced by real meshes — but a blocky bow that is actually in the character's hand communicates more than a perfect mesh that is not there.

functions.name: Rig.addTrail
functions.signature: Rig.addTrail(part: BasePart, color: Color3, length: number)
functions.summary: A trail that starts disabled. Anim markers switch it on for the swing window, which is what makes a strike read as a strike instead of a teleporting arm.

functions.name: Rig.stripDefaultAnimate
functions.summary: Hand a character's joints over to Forge. Roblox drives a character through two things, and stopping only the first is not enough: * the `Animate` script, which decides *which* animation to play; * the Humanoid's `Animator`, which evaluates animations and writes the This used to destroy the script and merely stop the playing tracks. On a Motor6D rig that was survivable: Roblox and Forge write different properties. On Roblox's current R15 player rig the joints are `AnimationConstraint`, both systems write the same `Transform`, and the Animator resets it to rest every single frame. The result was a player standing perfectly still while every clip in the engine played correctly into a value that was overwritten microseconds later. Measured: with the Animator present, 30 of 30 samples read identity. With it removed, 30 of 30 carried the pose. No render priority is late enough to win that fight -- the Animator has to go. The trade-off is real and worth stating: a character stripped this way cannot play Roblox `AnimationTrack`s any more. For a game animating procedurally that is the point. For one that wants both, do not call this.
examples: joints.

The first version of this file only had `Rig.describe(model)`, so the snapshot invoked it with nil and every reading came back as "attempt to index nil with 'GetDescendants'". The seam caught it on the first real read, which is exactly what the seam is for.

detail.name: Rng
detail.summary: Rng — seeded randomness in named streams. This is where determinism belongs, and the only place Forge insists on it. One shared Random is a trap: the moment loot rolls consume numbers from the same sequence as terrain, regenerating the same world with a different drop becomes impossible, and a bug reproduced yesterday will not reproduce today. Streams fix that — `Rng.stream("world")` and `Rng.stream("loot")` are independent, both derived from one master seed, both reproducible. The validation half can capture `Rng.describe()` with a run and replay it.
examples:
Rng.seed(20260819)
local world = Rng.stream("world")
local h = world:number(0, 1)

detail.name: Save
detail.summary: Save — player profiles that survive, migrate and do not corrupt. Three failures this exists to prevent, all of which are invisible in Studio and expensive in production: 1. No session lock. Two servers hold the same profile, the second one saves last, and a player loses an evening of progress. 2. No migration. You add a field, every returning player has `nil` where a number should be, and a dozen systems break in ways that look unrelated. 3. No retry, no BindToClose. The server shuts down mid-write and the save is simply gone.
examples:
Save.onLoaded:Connect(function(player, profile) ... end)
local profile = Save.get(player)

functions.name: Save.backups
functions.summary: Backups a game can offer to a player or a moderator. Returned newest first, with the timestamp and whether each one still verifies — a backup that fails its own checksum is worse than none, because restoring it looks like it worked.

functions.name: Save.rollback
functions.summary: Restore one. The current profile becomes a backup first, so a rollback is itself undoable — a rollback that destroys the thing it replaced is how a support ticket becomes two.

functions.name: Save.observe
functions.summary: Connect to onLoaded AND replay it for everyone already loaded. This exists because of a bug that cost a session: in Studio the local player joins at server start, so `Save.start()` loads and fires `onLoaded` while the bootstrap is still setting up. A listener connected forty lines later — after terrain generation, say — never hears it, no character ever spawns, and the game looks like it simply did not run. `onLoaded:Connect` has that hazard by construction. `observe` does not, so prefer it for anything that must happen once per player.

functions.name: Save.await
functions.summary: Waits for the profile, with a timeout. Any system that needs a profile on join should call this rather than assuming load order.

detail.name: Scene
detail.summary: Scene — a place expressed as data, not as code. Why this matters more than it looks ----------------------------------- A world built by a `for` loop in a server script exists only while that script runs. Nothing can list it, diff it, hand-edit it, or hand it to a tool. The moment the same world is a table of placements, all four become possible — including an editor, which is only ever a UI over this data. Scenes also make unloading real. `scene:unload()` removes exactly what the scene created and nothing else, which is what lets a game move between areas without leaking the previous one into the next.
examples:
local dungeon = Scene.create("Dungeon")
dungeon:add("Prop.Torch", CFrame.new(10, 3, 0))
dungeon:add("Enemy.Orc", CFrame.new(20, 3, 4), { tags = { "guard" } })
dungeon:spawnPoint("entrance", CFrame.new(0, 4, 0))
dungeon:load()

local saved = dungeon:serialize()   -- JSON-able; store it anywhere
Scene.fromTable(saved):load()

detail.name: Sched
detail.summary: Sched — how work gets spread across frames. Two failure modes this exists to prevent: 1. One `RunService.Heartbeat:Connect` per entity. Two hundred wolves become two hundred connections, each paying dispatch overhead, none of them aware of the frame budget. Use a `group` and tick them together. 2. Generation loops that run to completion and freeze the server for eight seconds. Use `budgeted` and the work yields when the frame gets expensive.

functions.name: Group:setSlices
functions.summary: slices > 1 spreads the group over N frames: 4 slices means each member is updated every 4th tick, and each frame only pays a quarter of the cost.

functions.summary: ============================= budgeted work ================================ Runs `fn(i)` for i = 1..count, yielding whenever the frame budget is spent. Terrain generation, prop scattering, save migration — anything long.

functions.name: Sched.drain
