functions.name: Sched.deferred
functions.summary: Coalesces bursts into one call at the end of the frame. For "state changed, resync the client" paths that would otherwise fire twelve times in a tick.

detail.name: Signal
detail.summary: !strict Signal — Lua-side event. Cheaper than BindableEvent and it does not serialise values, so tables cross a Fire by reference and identity survives.

functions.name: Signal:Fire
functions.summary: Handlers run on their own threads: one erroring listener never stops the rest, and a listener that yields never stalls the firer.

functions.name: Signal:FireSync
functions.summary: Same, but synchronous: use when order and completion matter more than isolation (a damage pipeline, for instance).

detail.name: Sky
detail.summary: Visual.Sky — the "shader pack" layer. What people mean by a Minecraft shader pack is not one effect. It is five things arriving together, and Roblox can do all five — most projects just never turn them on: 1. Real shadows. `Lighting.Technology = Future` is the single biggest 2. A sun that reads as a light source. Large angular size, strong glare, 3. Volumetric clouds. One `Clouds` instance under Terrain, and a flat sky 4. Water that reflects and moves. 5. A day that actually passes, with colour grading keyed to the hour The cycle interpolates every property together. A dawn where the fog warms before the ambient does looks broken in a way nobody can name, which is why this drives one blend across a keyframe table instead of tweening each effect on its own schedule.
examples:
lever there is, and it is the one setting that cannot be changed from
a script: it has to be in the place file. Everything below looks flat
without it.
god rays through the haze.
becomes a sky.
rather than one look bolted on.

Sky.install()                       -- sky, clouds, water
Sky.cycle({ minutesPerDay = 20 })   -- and time starts moving

functions.name: Sky.install
functions.summary: Sky, clouds and water. Idempotent, so calling it twice is harmless. `Lighting.Technology` is read-only at runtime and raises a capability error if even *read* from an ordinary script, so it is not touched here — it goes in the project file. This function warns when the place is not on Future, because every value below was chosen for it.

functions.name: Sky.applyHour
functions.summary: Turn a blended key into a `Visual` look and apply it, so quality tiers and everything else in Visual keep working.

functions.name: Sky.pin
functions.summary: Hold a fixed hour against replication. `setHour` alone loses: Lighting replicates from the server, so the place file's `ClockTime` lands *after* an early client write and silently wins. The symptom is a sky stuck at whatever the project file says while the code insists it set golden hour — which is exactly what happened here. A cycle does not have this problem because it rewrites every frame. A pinned look needs to notice and reassert.

detail.name: Spring
detail.summary: Spring — damped harmonic motion for numbers and Vector3. Why this exists: tweens are for things that must arrive on a schedule (a menu sliding in). Springs are for things that must feel physical (a camera catching up, a weapon settling after a swing, a health bar overshooting). Almost everything an agent reaches for a tween to do, in gameplay, wants a spring instead — and gets a better result for less code, because a spring survives being interrupted mid-flight.
examples:
local s = Spring.new(0, { frequency = 4, damping = 0.7 })
s:impulse(12)          -- kick it
s.goal = 30            -- retarget any time
local v = s:step(dt)   -- integrate, returns current value

functions.name: Spring:step
functions.summary: Semi-implicit Euler, clamped so a frame hitch cannot make it explode. Long frames are subdivided rather than integrated in one leap.

functions.name: Spring:reset
functions.summary: Teleport: no motion, no overshoot. Use on respawn, never mid-animation.

detail.name: Streaming
detail.summary: Streaming — a chunk layer over a Scene. Roblox's own StreamingEnabled streams *replication*: the server still holds every instance, and every instance still costs memory, physics and a slot in the DataModel. A scene with twelve thousand placements is twelve thousand instances on the server whether anyone is near them or not. This streams *existence*. Placements are bucketed into chunks; a chunk materialises when someone is near it and dematerialises when nobody is. The scene keeps all twelve thousand placements as data — a few hundred kilobytes of tables — and the world holds only what is being looked at. Two things this gets right that a naive version does not: * Load and unload radii differ. With one radius, a player standing on a * Materialisation is budgeted. Walking into a dense chunk otherwise
examples:
local streamer = Streaming.attach(scene, {
chunkSize = 128,
loadRadius = 320,
unloadRadius = 420,
budget = 12,
})
streamer:start()

boundary thrashes a chunk in and out every tick. Hysteresis is not a
refinement here, it is the difference between working and unusable.

creates four hundred instances in one frame and drops the server for
half a second, exactly when the player is moving fastest.

functions.name: StreamerClass:reindex
functions.summary: Rebuild the chunk index from the scene's placements. Cheap enough to call after bulk edits; the editor calls it every time a placement moves between chunks.

functions.name: StreamerClass:pin
functions.summary: Force a region in, regardless of anchors. For a cutscene, a teleport destination, or a headless measurement run that has no players in it.

functions.name: StreamerClass:loadAll
functions.summary: Materialise everything, ignoring anchors entirely. Used by the editor, where you must see what you are editing, and by a full-world validation pass.

detail.name: Telemetry
detail.summary: Telemetry — what actually happened, in a live game. `Debug.expose` answers questions in a Studio session. It cannot tell you that 3% of players never finish spawning, that the tutorial loses a third of people at step four, or that one error fires eleven thousand times a day from one line. This is the module that substitutes for judgement. An agent proposing a balance change is guessing; a funnel showing where players stop is evidence. Forge does not pick a destination. Open Cloud, an HTTP endpoint, a DataStore, or `print` in development — you register a sink and the buffering, batching, retry and error aggregation are handled.
examples:
Telemetry.sink(function(batch) ... end)     -- you choose the destination
Telemetry.event("salvage.opened", { kind = "hull", player = id })
Telemetry.funnel("onboarding", 3, subject)
Telemetry.mark(subject, "first_kill")

functions.name: Telemetry.sink
functions.summary: A sink returns true if it accepted the batch. A sink that returns false or errors keeps the batch buffered for the next flush, which is what stops a transient HTTP failure from silently deleting an hour of data.

functions.name: Telemetry.funnel
functions.signature: Telemetry.funnel(name: string, step: number, subject: string)
functions.summary: A funnel records the furthest step each subject reached. Recording every step transition instead would answer the same question with fifty times the volume, and the question is always "where do they stop".

functions.name: Telemetry.funnelReport
functions.summary: Drop-off per step: the shape a designer actually reads.

functions.name: Telemetry.mark
functions.summary: One-off milestones: first kill, first purchase, tutorial complete.

functions.name: Telemetry.printSink
functions.summary: A sink that prints, for development. Deliberately not the default: silently printing telemetry in production is how a game ships with no analytics and nobody noticing.

detail.name: Testing
detail.summary: Testing — assertions about a game that is actually running. Every other check in this project reads source. The compiler reads syntax, the doctor reads structure, the unit tests read text. None of them can tell you whether an attack lands, whether an enemy dies, or whether a save survives a rejoin — and those are the only questions that matter. So this runs inside the live game. It drives real characters through real systems and asserts on real state. Nothing here is mocked: a test that hits a fake enemy with a fake sword proves that the fakes agree with each other. --- Why bots and not mocks --------------------------------------------- A bot here is a real `Rig` with a real `Humanoid`, spawned into the real world, moved by the real movement code and damaged by the real damage pipeline. When one of these tests fails it is because the game is broken, not because a stub drifted. That is the entire point: this suite is the thing that was missing when every genuine bug in this project had to be found by a person watching a screen. --- Determinism --------------------------------------------------------- Scenarios are given their own RNG stream and their own container, and the world is put back afterwards. Two runs of the same suite see the same numbers, so a failure is reproducible rather than a story about one afternoon.
examples:
Testing.scenario("a third hit finishes a husk", function(t)
local enemy = t:spawnEnemy("husk", Vector3.new(0, 5, 0))
local hero = t:spawnBot(Vector3.new(0, 5, 6))

t:face(hero, enemy)
for _ = 1, 3 do
t:attack(hero)
t:wait(0.6)
end

t:expect(not Combat.isAlive(enemy), "the husk should be down")
end)
Testing.run()   -- returns a report a machine can read

functions.name: Context:track
functions.summary: Own an instance for the length of the scenario, and hold it still. Anchored, because a rig from `Rig.build` is unanchored and has a Humanoid: spawned at test altitude it falls, lands in the middle of whatever someone is playing, and is deleted a second later. That is exactly what it looks like from the player's seat — bodies dropping out of the sky and vanishing — and it is the test suite doing it. A scenario that genuinely needs physics unanchors what it spawned; that is one line and an explicit decision, which is the right way round.

functions.name: Context:spawnEnemy
functions.summary: A real enemy, built by the same code the game uses. Deliberately not a stub with a Health attribute: the value of this suite is that it exercises `Rig.build`, the Humanoid, the damage pipeline and every modifier the game installed. A stub would pass while the real thing was broken, which is the failure mode being designed out.

functions.name: Context:face
functions.summary: Point one model at another. Combat is directional almost everywhere, so a test that forgets this fails for the wrong reason.

functions.name: Context:waitUntil
functions.summary: Wait for something to become true, or give up. The alternative — a fixed sleep long enough for the slowest machine — makes a suite that is both slow and flaky. This is fast when the game is fast and still correct when it is not.

functions.name: Context:expectEqual
functions.signature: Context:expectEqual(actual: any, expected: any, message: string?)

functions.name: Context:expectNear
functions.signature: Context:expectNear(actual: number, expected: number, tolerance: number, message: string?)

functions.name: Testing.run
functions.summary: Run every registered scenario and report. Each case runs inside a coroutine with a deadline, because the most common way a live test fails is not an assertion but a hang: something waits for an event that a broken system never fires. A hang that takes the whole suite down teaches nothing; a hang reported as a timeout on one named scenario points straight at the break.

functions.name: Testing.publish
functions.summary: Publish the last report where a tool outside the game can read it. A StringValue under ReplicatedStorage, the same channel `Debug.expose` uses and for the same reason: it replicates, so it is readable from a play session that no edit-mode command can reach. The alternative — returning the report to a caller — only works if the caller is inside the same Lua VM, which a CLI never is.

functions.name: Testing.runAndPublish
functions.summary: Load a game's scenarios, run them, and publish the result. One call, so a game's bootstrap can opt in with a single line and a CLI has one thing to trigger.

detail.name: Trove
detail.summary: !strict Trove — one object owns everything it created, and releases all of it at once. Leaked `:Connect` handles are the number one cause of a Roblox project getting slower the longer a session runs. The fix is not discipline, it is making the cleanup path shorter than the leak path. Anything a system creates goes in a trove; the system's destroy is one line.

functions.name: Trove:add
functions.summary: add(object [, methodName]) -> object   (returns what you passed, so it chains)

functions.name: Trove:task
functions.summary: A per-frame job that dies with the trove. `phase` is "render" (client only), "stepped" or "heartbeat" (default).

functions.name: Trove:clean
functions.summary: Releases in reverse order of addition, so a thing always outlives what it depends on.

detail.name: UI
detail.summary: UI — tokens and widgets, so an interface looks designed instead of assembled. Agent-built Roblox UI has a signature: default fonts, primary-colour backgrounds, no consistent spacing, every panel a slightly different grey. The cause is not bad taste, it is that every widget gets invented at the point of use with whatever numbers were in mind at that second. Tokens fix that. Read colours and spacing from `UI.theme`, never literals, and a whole interface stays coherent even when twelve different systems built pieces of it.
examples:
local gui = UI.mount("HUD")
local panel = UI.panel(gui, { size = UDim2.fromOffset(320, 96), pos = ... })
local hp = UI.bar(panel, { color = UI.theme.color.danger })
hp:set(0.62)
UI.toast("Level 7 reached", { color = UI.theme.color.gold })

functions.name: UI.bar
functions.summary: A bar with a delayed trail. The trail is the whole point: it shows how much damage just landed, which is information the player cannot get from a bar that simply jumps to its new value.

functions.name: UI.button

detail.name: Ui
detail.summary: Editor.Ui — the overlay. Deliberately thin. Every button sends the same operation an agent would send, so there is no behaviour here that automation cannot reach — the UI is a view, never a second implementation. Click an asset to arm it, click the world to place. Click a placed thing to select it. Arrows nudge, R rotates, G drops it on the ground, Delete removes.
examples:
local EditorUi = require(ReplicatedStorage.Forge.Editor.Ui)
EditorUi.mount()          -- F4 toggles it

functions.name: Ui.setMode
functions.summary: Switching mode is a client concern: the handles are client instances and the server has no opinion about which one is showing. Everything a mode *does* still goes through the same server ops.

detail.name: Visual
detail.summary: Visual — art direction as data. Why a generated Roblox game looks generated ------------------------------------------- It is almost never the geometry. It is four things, and all four are defaults nobody changed: 1. Default Lighting. Flat white ambient, no atmosphere, fog off. Every 2. Primary colours. `BrickColor.Random()` or hand-picked RGB per system, 3. No post. No bloom, no colour grading, no depth cue. 4. SmoothPlastic on everything, which reads as plastic because it is. A "look" here bundles all four into one named, tunable thing: And a palette makes procedural colour cohere instead of scatter: Quality tiers ------------- Half of Roblox is on a phone that cannot take three post-processing effects and shadow maps. `Visual.autoQuality()` reads the device and drops what costs most, in the order that costs the least to lose visually.
examples: world lit identically, so every world reads identically.
so nothing shares a palette and everything fights.

Visual.defineLook("drowned_night", { ... })
Visual.apply("drowned_night")
Visual.transition("dawn", 6)

local palette = Visual.palette("shore")
part.Color = palette:pick("stone", 0.4)

functions.name: Visual.transition
functions.summary: Blend from the current look to another over `seconds`. Not a Tween: half of a look is Atmosphere and post-effect properties across four different instances, and driving them from one interpolation keeps them in step. A dawn where the fog arrives before the ambient does looks broken in a way nobody can name.

functions.name: Visual.capture
functions.summary: Snapshot the live Lighting state in Look shape, so a transition can start from whatever is on screen rather than from a named look.

functions.name: Visual.autoQuality
functions.summary: Pick a tier from the device. Roblox exposes no reliable GPU signal, so this reads what it can: touch without a mouse is a phone, a small viewport is a phone, and everything else gets the benefit of the doubt. Wrong in the generous direction on a tablet, which is the cheap mistake; wrong in the stingy direction on a desktop would be the expensive one.

functions.name: Palette:pick
functions.summary: Sample a ramp at 0..1, interpolating between stops.

functions.name: Palette:vary
functions.signature: Palette:vary(ramp: string, alpha: number, amount: number?)
functions.summary: Sample with a small hue/value jitter, so a hundred rocks are a family rather than a hundred copies.

functions.name: Visual.dress
functions.signature: Visual.dress(instance: Instance, family: string, alpha: number?, paletteName: string?)
functions.summary: Dress an instance from a palette family in one call.

detail.name: Weapon
detail.summary: Weapon — the layer between "the player pressed fire" and "something took damage". Combat already knows how to fly a projectile and how to apply damage. What was missing is everything in between: how often a weapon may fire, where the shot actually goes when the barrel is not perfectly still, how many rounds are left, and what happens while reloading. Those rules are the same for every shooter ever made, which is exactly why they belong here and not in the game. What this module does NOT decide: what a weapon is called, what it costs, who may hold it, what it looks like, or whether your game even has guns. It gives you numbers and a verdict; the game decides what they mean. --- Determinism, and why it matters ------------------------------------- Spread is generated from a seed, not from `math.random`. `Weapon.fire` returns the seed it used, so a client that predicts a shot and the server that resolves it produce the *same* pellet pattern from the same number. Without that, every shotgun blast disagrees between the two machines and you get corrections on every trigger pull. --- No update loop ------------------------------------------------------ Spread recovery, recoil decay and reload completion are all computed from timestamps when someone asks, never on a heartbeat. A hundred idle weapons cost nothing, because an idle weapon genuinely has nothing to do.
examples:
Weapon.define("longbow", {
mode = "projectile",
damage = 46, rpm = 55, range = 700,
charge = { time = 0.85, minRatio = 0.3 },
magazine = 1, reserve = math.huge, reloadTime = 0.55,
projectile = { speed = 190, gravity = 42 },
})
Weapon.equip(character, "longbow")

local shot = Weapon.fire(character, muzzle, aimDirection, {
ignore = { character },
onHit = function(model, position, normal) ... end,
})
if not shot.ok then
-- shot.reason is "cooldown" | "empty" | "reloading" | "no-weapon"
end

functions.name: Weapon.define
functions.summary: Register a weapon. Definitions are data and are meant to be reloaded: call `define` again with the same id and every weapon already in someone's hands picks up the new numbers, which is what makes tuning a weapon a five-second loop instead of a restart.

functions.name: Weapon.equip
functions.summary: Give a character a weapon. Equipping the same id twice is a no-op rather than a reset, so a game that calls this defensively every frame does not silently refill the magazine.

functions.name: Weapon.reloadProgress
functions.summary: How far through the reload we are, 0 to 1. Exists so a progress ring on the HUD does not have to duplicate the timing maths and drift out of sync with the weapon it is describing.

functions.name: Weapon.beginCharge
functions.summary: Draw weapons — bows, railguns, anything where holding the button matters. A charge is just a timestamp. The ratio is read at the moment of release and multiplies damage and projectile speed, so a half-drawn bow is genuinely weaker rather than merely slower to animate.

functions.name: Weapon.chargeRatio
functions.summary: How far the weapon is drawn, 0 to 1. Reports the truth, including zero. An earlier version floored this at `minRatio`, which quietly made the "undercharged" refusal in `fire` unreachable: a client that never started a draw got a 30% shot instead of nothing. The floor belongs at the gate, not in the measurement.

functions.name: Weapon.spreadDirection
functions.signature: Weapon.spreadDirection(direction: Vector3, degrees: number, seed: number, index: number)
functions.summary: Deterministic cone. The same seed and index always produce the same direction, which is what lets the client draw a tracer that lands where the server says it landed. `math.random` here would be a desync per pellet.

functions.name: Weapon.fire
functions.signature: Weapon.fire(owner: Model, origin: Vector3, direction: Vector3, options: any?)
functions.summary: Pull the trigger. Always returns a table. `ok = false` with a `reason` is the normal way a weapon says no — refusing by returning nil would make every caller write the same nil check and lose the reason, which is the part the HUD wants. Options: ignore   instances the shot passes through (the shooter, usually) seed     supply one to reproduce a shot exactly; omit and one is made onHit    called per pellet that connects: (model?, position, normal, damage) onSpawn  projectile mode only, called with each projectile made filter   projectile mode only, forwarded to Combat

functions.name: Weapon.recoil
functions.summary: The recoil the camera should be showing right now, in degrees. Read it every frame and add it to the aim angles; it decays on its own, so there is nothing to reset and nothing to leak if the player stops firing.

functions.name: Weapon.describe
functions.summary: What a validator reads to prove a shooting game actually has weapons.

detail.name: Weather
detail.summary: Weather — conditions that change while people are playing. `Visual` and `Sky` decide what a world looks like at an hour. Neither has any notion of a world that is *currently* raining, or of one condition giving way to another over a minute rather than a cut. That gap is why the engine's outdoor worlds have exactly one mood each. What a condition is here: a set of target values for the sky, the atmosphere and the particle layer, plus how long it takes to get there. Nothing snaps. A storm that arrives instantly reads as a bug in the lighting; a storm that takes forty seconds reads as weather. --- Client-side, deliberately ------------------------------------------- Lighting replicates from the server, so a server that drives weather fights every client's own atmosphere and loses the race half the time — this project has already spent an afternoon on exactly that with the day cycle. The server decides *which* condition is in force and tells clients; each client renders it. That also means rain is one client's particle budget rather than the server's replication budget.
examples:
Weather.set("storm")
Weather.cycle({ "clear", "overcast", "rain" })

functions.name: Weather.installDefaults
functions.summary: A starting set, so a world has weather before anybody authors any. Deliberately mild. A default that ships a thunderstorm makes every game built on this engine look like the same game, which is the failure this project exists to avoid — these are the neutral ends of a range, not a style.

functions.name: Weather.set
functions.summary: Put a condition in force. `immediate` skips the transition, which is for loading into a world that is already raining rather than for gameplay: a cut between conditions is the one thing that makes weather look scripted.

functions.name: Weather.cycle
functions.summary: Move through a sequence of conditions. Weather that changes on a timer is the cheapest way to make a world feel like it exists independently of the player, and the whole cost is one coroutine that sleeps.

detail.name: World
detail.summary: World — terrain as a composable function, not a fixed generator. A heightfield here is a stack of layers you declare. Forge does not know what an island is; it knows how to add noise, ridges, basins and flats together and how to turn the result into voxels without freezing the server. The material function is where biomes live, and it is yours. Forge never ships a biome table, because a biome table is a game.
examples:
local hf = World.heightfield({
size = 1024,
seed = 20260819,
base = { { frequency = 0.0018, octaves = 4, weight = 0.60 },
{ frequency = 0.0074, octaves = 5, weight = 0.32 },
{ frequency = 0.0280, octaves = 3, weight = 0.08 } },
range = { 4, 96 },
falloff = { power = 2.7 },
features = {
{ kind = "ridge", center = Vector2.new(-320, 305), radius = 300, amount = 118, sharpness = 1.7 },
{ kind = "basin", center = Vector2.new(255, -290), radius = 190, amount = 26 },
{ kind = "flat",  center = Vector2.new(0, 0),      radius = 90,  height = 36, blend = 1.9 },
},
})

functions.name: Heightfield:slope
functions.signature: Heightfield:slope(x: number, z: number, epsilon: number?)
functions.summary: Surface normal's Y component by finite difference. 1 = flat, 0 = vertical.

functions.name: Heightfield:normal
functions.signature: Heightfield:normal(x: number, z: number, epsilon: number?)

functions.name: Heightfield:point
functions.signature: Heightfield:point(x: number, z: number, offsetY: number?)

functions.name: World.paint
functions.summary: Writes the heightfield into Roblox terrain. Two details that matter and are easy to get wrong: 1. Occupancy is a linear ramp across the surface voxel, not 0/1. Binary occupancy produces visible stair-stepping on every slope in the game. 2. Each chunk computes its own vertical extent. A flat meadow chunk writes ten voxels of height instead of fifty, which is the difference between a world that generates in eight seconds and one that generates in forty.

functions.name: World.scatter
functions.summary: Places things on the surface with a density function. Deterministic for a given seed, because placement uses a per-cell stream. Regenerating the world puts the same tree in the same place.

functions.name: World.surface
functions.signature: World.surface(x: number, z: number, options: any?)
functions.summary: ============================== surface queries ============================= The heightfield is the plan; this is the ground that actually exists. Use it for anything that must stand on the world after it was written, because voxel rounding means the two differ by up to half a voxel.

functions.name: World.findGround
functions.signature: World.findGround(around: Vector3, radius: number, options: any?)
functions.summary: Finds standable ground near a point: what a spawner should call instead of trusting a heightfield value on a cliff face.
